title: The full bath
hook: a full wash after intimacy, after menstruation, before Friday and Eid

segments.voice: Yesterday, what breaks wudu, and your line: renew it. What did you start fresh instead of arguing with it? Wudu washes some limbs. Today, the wash that covers everything. Day one thousand seventy-six.

Friday morning, early. The kettle's on, the kids are still asleep, and a father stands in the shower a little longer than usual. He isn't lingering. He's working through an order: hands first, then the wudu he knows by heart, then water through the roots of his hair, then over his head, then over the whole body, right side, left side, until nothing is left dry. Later he'll put on his good shirt and go to the Friday prayer. To anyone passing the bathroom door, it's just a shower. To him it has a name, and a set of steps that comes from a description kept in the hadith.
screen: `FRIDAY MORNING, EARLY.` → `A SHOWER WITH AN ORDER.` → `UNTIL NOTHING IS LEFT DRY.`

segments.voice: The name is ghusl, the full bath. Where wudu washes certain limbs, ghusl reaches the whole body. The Qur'an names it in the same verse that gives wudu, 5:6, and Pickthall's translation puts it simply: "And if ye are unclean, purify yourselves." The fiqh books list when ghusl is required. After sexual intimacy. After a woman's menstruation ends, and after the bleeding that follows childbirth. Without it, the prayer waits. Then there are times when it's recommended, a gift rather than a duty. Before the Friday prayer: in Sahih al-Bukhari, number 877, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says that whoever comes to the Friday prayer should bathe first. Scholars discuss whether that wording makes it required or strongly recommended. And before the Eid prayers, which reports say companions of the Prophet ﷺ did. Now the steps. In Sahih al-Bukhari, number 248, Aishah describes how the Prophet ﷺ bathed. He began by washing his hands. Then he made wudu as for prayer. Then he put his fingers into the water and ran them through the roots of his hair. Then he poured water over his head, three handfuls. Then he let water flow over his whole body. That's the full sunnah form. Scholars explain that the minimum is less: the intention, and water reaching the whole body, with the schools differing on whether rinsing the mouth and nose belongs to that minimum. So yes, a shower can be a ghusl. What turns it into one is the intention and the care that no part is skipped.
screen: `GHUSL REACHES THE WHOLE BODY.` · `REQUIRED: AFTER INTIMACY, AFTER BLEEDING.` · `RECOMMENDED: BEFORE FRIDAY AND EID.` · `AISHAH'S DESCRIPTION, STEP BY STEP.` · then, large: `AND IF YE ARE UNCLEAN, PURIFY YOURSELVES.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn the steps by walking through them, without water. Settle, and breathe. Picture your hands being washed. Then, in your mind, the wudu, limb by limb. Then fingers moving through the roots of your hair. Then water poured over your head. Then water running over your shoulders, your back, down to your feet, right side, then left, until nothing is left dry. Go slowly enough that you'd notice a missed spot. If you make ghusl, you can carry this order into your next one. The bell holds the time.
Ghusl. The full bath: required after intimacy and after menstruation, recommended before Friday and Eid, done with intention and nothing left dry. Today's word.
Your line: the whole body clean. Today, take your next shower in order, slowly, as a beginning rather than a chore. Tomorrow, when there's no water. Day one thousand seventy-six.

howItsDone: Muslims make ghusl, a full-body wash with intention, after intimacy and after menstruation or postnatal bleeding before praying again, and as a recommended bath before the Friday prayer and the Eid prayers, following the steps Aishah described.
